summary: This memo defines a Remote-ID option for DHCPv6 relay agents. It is the DHCPv6 counterpart of the Remote-ID suboption in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Option from RFC 3046, and lets a relay identify the remote end of a connection to the server.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper passing messages to the address office can add a note saying which door the request came from. This is that note for the newer version of the address-giving system.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 remote-id option
what does a dhcpv6 relay agent do
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 relay agent tells the server which remote user, port or circuit a request came from.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv6 server sometimes needs to know which remote host or circuit a relayed request arrived on, for example to pick settings for a particular subscriber.
tldr.mechanism: The relay agent adds a Remote-ID option (option code 37) to the relayed message. It holds a vendor enterprise number plus an opaque remote-id value that the server treats as one exact-match string.
tldr.outcome: It is the DHCPv6 equivalent of the Remote-ID suboption in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Option. The information is only as trustworthy as the relay agent's own source for it.

today: RFC 4649 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the available metadata.

sections.title: Why a Relay Adds Information
sections.content:
DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) gives IPv6 clients addresses and configuration. It includes a relay agent capability: processes in the network infrastructure receive multicast messages from clients and relay them to DHCPv6 servers. In some networks it is useful for the relay to add information to the message before passing it on.

A server can use that information when deciding which addresses, delegated prefixes and configuration parameters a client should get. This memo defines the DHCPv6 equivalent of the Remote-ID suboption of the DHCPv4 Relay Agent option from RFC 3046. The motivation and usage scenarios are described there, not repeated here.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the helper in the middle knows something the address office would like to know. This note lets the helper pass it along.

sections.title: The Remote-ID Option Format
sections.content:
The option has four parts: OPTION_REMOTE_ID (the option code), option-len, a 32-bit enterprise-number and a variable-length remote-id.

The option code is 37. The option-len is 4 plus the length, in octets, of the remote-id field, so the minimum option-len is 5 octets. The enterprise number is the vendor's registered Enterprise Number as registered with IANA. The remote-id is an opaque value.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a label saying what kind of note it is, a length, the name of the company that made the helper, and then the actual identifying text.

sections.title: What the Remote-ID Contains
sections.content:
What the remote-id means is vendor specific, and the enterprise-number field says which vendor. The RFC suggests it may encode, for instance, a caller ID telephone number for a dial-up connection, a user name prompted for by a Remote Access Server, a remote caller ATM address, a modem ID of a cable data modem, the remote IP address of a point-to-point link, a remote X.25 address, or an interface or port identifier.

The enterprise-number followed by the remote-id must be globally unique, so each vendor must ensure the remote-id is unique within its own enterprise number. One suggested way is to include the relay agent's DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID) in the remote-id. The option may be added by relay agents that terminate switched or permanent circuits and can identify the remote host end of the circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The note can say things like a phone number or a port number. To make sure two notes are never confused, it starts with the name of the company that wrote it.

sections.title: Relay and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 relay agent may be configured to include a Remote-ID option in the relayed (RELAY-FORW) messages it sends.

A server that is configured to support the option may use it to select parameters specific to particular users, hosts or subscriber modems. The server SHOULD treat the combined enterprise-number and remote-id as one opaque value and base policies on exact string match only. It SHOULD NOT parse the remote-id field internally. There is no requirement that a server return the option and its data in a RELAY-REPLY message.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper may add the note. The address office reads it as one single label and only checks whether it matches exactly, without trying to understand the inside.

sections.title: How Far the Information Can Be Trusted
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 3315 section 21.1 on securing messages between servers and relay agents, and section 23 on general DHCPv6 security. RFC 3046 discusses how this information can enhance trust in some environments.

Even if the server trusts the relay agent not to modify the option, its confidence in the data is no higher than the relay's own confidence in the information it put there. In some protocols a client may be able to spoof or choose port identifiers, caller ID information or other data carried in the option. Sites should weigh that risk when deciding what uses of the option are appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is only as honest as what the helper was told. If someone can fib to the helper, the note will carry the fib.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA has assigned DHCPv6 option code 37 for the Relay Agent Remote-ID Option. The enterprise-number field refers to the IANA registry of Private Enterprise Numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number list now has the number 37 reserved for this kind of note.

fields.name: option-len
fields.desc: 4 plus the length of remote-id in octets; minimum 5.

fields.name: enterprise-number
fields.desc: The vendor's registered Enterprise Number from IANA.
